newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EIA lowers energy price outlook for 2015.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EIA lowers energy price outlook for 2015.

text.p: New technology, expanded production and lower U.S. transportation and distribution costs should keep energy prices lower than previously expected over the next 19 years, the Energy Information Administration said Wednesday in its 1997 Annual Energy Outlook.
The weaker prices were expected to boost U.S. demand for energy from 91 quadrillion BTUs in 1995 to 111 quads in 2015, 3 quads more than previously forecast.
EIA projected world oil prices would average $21 a barrel in 2015, lowering its previous forecast for 2015 by $5. Those prices were up from $17.26 in 1995.
The softer oil price forecast reflected EIA's view that production from OPEC countries would grow and technology would advance to maintain production levels in non-OPEC countries.
It assumed Iraq would not resume production until 1998 and would step up to full capacity in 2000.
The forecasts were based on expected U.S. annual gross domestic product growth of 1.9 percent over the 1995 to 2015 forecast period.
With the weaker oil prices, EIA lowered its projection for U.S. oil production in 2015 to 5.2 million barrels per day from 5.8 million bpd, and down from 6.6 million bpd in 1995.
As a result of lower U.S. production, net oil imports were expected to climb to 13.5 million bpd or 61 percent of U.S. consumption in 2015, up from 44 percent in 1995.
Total U.S. oil consumption was seen at 22.1 million bpd in 2015, up from 17.73 million bpd in 1995.

Natural gas prices at the wellhead were pegged to rise from $1.61 per thousand cubic feet in 1995 to $2.13 in 2015, down from last year's forecast of $2.63, based on a reevaluation of technological advances.

"(N)atural gas production is increased, with less drilling activity and at lower cost, particularly in offshore regions, where technological progress has a greater impact on the development of relatively immature fields," EIA said.
Production was expected to grow at 1.7 percent a year on average from 1995 to reach 26.1 trillion cubic feet in 2015.
At the same time, coal prices were seen falling to $15.46 per ton in 2015, down from a previous forecast of $17.75.
EIA linked the lower minemouth coal prices to a rise in productivity, a shift to cheaper western production as transportation costs fell, and a drop in labor costs.
Coal production was projected to rise 1.0 percent a year from 1995 through 2015 to 1.27 billion tons, largely to meet U.S. consumption.
EIA said lower fossil fuel prices and new competition in power markets should keep average electricity prices 0.8 cents below its previous forecast at 6.3 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2015.
Lower fuel prices, especially for natural gas, were expected to "delay the penetration of some renewable technologies," EIA said.
As a result, renewable energy production, including hydropower, would rise from 6.3 quads in 1995 to 7.7 quads in 2015, down 0.8 quads from the previous forecast for 2015.

With about 38 percent of current U.S. nuclear power capacity expected to be retired by 2015 as plant operating licenses expire, electricity generation demand for natural gas and coal was expected to rise sharply, EIA said.
Although coal would remain the dominant fuel in power generation, EIA projected that by 2015 natural gas would triple its share of the market to 29 percent.
EIA released the first part of its 1997 long-term outlook earlier than normal, and said it would release the rest of its projections on December 18.
